To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
stomata respond to the humidity of the air surrounding the guard cells and that this response is not the result of water transfer from the epidermis.

stomata respond to water vapour pressure gradients across the epidermis and that stomatal apertures are consistent with water potential equilibration between the guard cells, the water vapour in the pore and the air outside the epidermis.

stomata of isolated epidermis hydrate and dehydate entirely from water vapours in the air, and that this response is consistent with the stomatal aperture being determined by water potential equilibrium between guard cells and air near the bottom the stomatal pore.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the stomatal response to humidity, and the stomatal responses to changes in air humidity are mediated by changes in the water potential of the guard cells.
the mechanism of stomatal responses to environmental humidity.
the role of humidity in stomatal responses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

stomata in leaves respond to the water potential of the air outside the leaf, but that the response in isolated epidermis is the result of water vapour exchange between the guard cells of the stomata and the air near their pore.
the stomata of Tradescantiae and Viciae are able to sense and respond to humidity in an air stream.

the guard cells are able to hydrate and to dehydrate from the air in the absence of living epidermal cells, but that the stomata are unlikely to respond to changes in the humidity of the air in the same way in vivo.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
stomata in Tradescantia are able to hydrate and desiccate from the surrounding atmosphere, and that the responses of isolated epidermes and intact leaves to humidity are qualitatively the same.

guard cells are able to respond to the vapour pressure of air in the immediate vicinity of the stomatal pores, and that this response is the result of the water potential equilibrium of the guard cells and air near the bottom part of the stomatal aperture.
stomatal responses to relative humidity in intact leaves are not the result of water vapour exchange between the guard cells, the air near the stomatal pore and the air in the substomatal cavity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
stomata respond directly to the water potential of the air near the stomata.

the stomatal response to humidity in isolated guard cells is a direct result of water potential equilibration between the guard cells, the air near the stomatal pore bottom, and the air outside the leaf.
stomata are able to hydrate and dry out in response to changes in the water vapour concentration around the leaf, and this response is not dependent on living cells in the epidermis.
